final_note: You worked through D1.3 Mutation and gene editing — 10 guide statements.

concepts.def: A structural change to a gene at the molecular level: a change in the base sequence of the DNA that makes up the gene. Gene mutations are classified as substitutions, insertions or deletions. They are distinct from chromosome mutations, which change the number or structure of whole chromosomes.
A gene mutation in which one base in the DNA sequence is replaced by a different base, so that the number of bases in the gene is unchanged. Only the codon containing the substituted base is altered.
A gene mutation in which one or more extra bases are added to the base sequence of a gene, making the gene longer. All bases after the insertion point are displaced along the sequence.
A gene mutation in which one or more bases are removed from the base sequence of a gene, making the gene shorter. All bases after the deletion point move up to fill the gap.

A position in the genome at which different individuals in a population carry different bases as a result of a base substitution mutation that has spread in the population. SNPs are the commonest form of genetic variation; most lie in non-coding DNA, and those within genes may or may not change an amino acid.

The property of the genetic code that most amino acids are coded for by more than one codon (64 codons code for 20 amino acids and three stop signals). Because of degeneracy, a base substitution that converts a codon into another codon for the same amino acid has no effect on the polypeptide.

A base substitution changes at most one codon in the mRNA. It may leave the amino acid unchanged (a silent, or synonymous, substitution, because of degeneracy), change a single amino acid in the polypeptide, or convert an amino acid codon into a stop codon so that translation ends early and the polypeptide is shortened. The reading frame is not altered.

The consequence of an insertion or deletion of a number of bases that is not a multiple of three: every codon after the mutation is read in a shifted frame, so the amino acid sequence from that point onwards is changed and a premature stop codon is likely to be reached. A frameshifted polypeptide is very likely to cease to function.

The addition or loss of a long stretch of bases within a gene. Even if the number of bases is a multiple of three and the reading frame is preserved, many amino acids are added to or missing from the polypeptide, so it is unlikely to fold into a functional shape and is likely to cease functioning.

A chemical or physical agent that increases the frequency of gene mutation by damaging DNA or by interfering with DNA replication. Chemical mutagens and mutagenic forms of radiation are the two categories; mutations also arise without any mutagen through errors in DNA replication or repair.

A chemical that reacts with DNA or is incorporated into it so that bases are altered or mispaired during replication. Examples include benzo[a]pyrene and other polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons in tobacco smoke, nitrosamines, mustard gas and nitrous acid. Many chemical mutagens are also carcinogens.

Radiation with enough energy to break or chemically alter DNA. Ionizing radiation (X-rays, gamma rays and the alpha and beta particles emitted by radioactive isotopes) breaks DNA strands and damages bases; ultraviolet (UV) light causes adjacent thymine bases to bond to each other, distorting the helix. Lower-energy radiation such as visible light, microwaves and radio waves is not mutagenic.

concepts.term: Errors in DNA replication and repair
concepts.def: A source of gene mutation that needs no mutagen. DNA polymerase occasionally pairs a base incorrectly during replication; most such errors are corrected by proofreading and by DNA repair enzymes, but a small fraction escape and become permanent changes in the base sequence. Faults in the repair process itself can also introduce or fail to remove errors.

Mutations can occur at any position in the base sequence of a genome, and which base changes is not determined by whether the change would be useful to the organism. No natural mechanism is known that makes a deliberate change to a particular base with the purpose of altering a trait.

A position or type of sequence in the genome at which the probability of mutation is higher than average. For example, cytosine bases that carry a methyl group change to thymine far more often than other bases, so some bases have a higher probability of mutating than others even though mutation is random with respect to its usefulness.

A mutation in a cell of the germ line, that is in a gamete or in a cell that gives rise to gametes. Because the mutated gene is present in the gamete, it can be passed to the offspring and will then be present in every cell of the offspring, so germ cell mutations are inherited and add to the genetic variation of the species.

A mutation in a body cell that does not form gametes. It is copied only into the descendants of that cell within the individual, so it is not passed to offspring. Its consequences are confined to the individual in which it occurs, and in some cases lead to cancer.

concepts.term: Cancer as a consequence of somatic mutation
concepts.def: Cancer arises when mutations accumulate in the genes of a somatic cell that control the cell cycle and cell division, so that the cell divides uncontrollably to form a tumour. Because these mutations are in somatic cells, the cancer itself is not inherited by offspring, although germ cell mutations that raise the risk of cancer can be.

concepts.term: Mutation as the original source of genetic variation
concepts.def: New alleles arise only by gene mutation; meiosis and fertilization reshuffle existing alleles but cannot create new ones. Most mutations are harmful or neutral for the individual in which they occur, but in a species over the long term mutation is essential because it supplies the variation on which natural selection acts.

A test sold directly to consumers that reads variants (mainly SNPs) in a person's DNA and reports associations with potential future health and disease risk. Without expert interpretation the results can be problematic: an association indicates altered probability, not certainty, and it does not diagnose present disease or take account of other genes, environment and lifestyle.

A technique for investigating the function of a gene by changing the gene so that it is inoperative (no functional product is made) and then comparing the phenotype of the knockout organism with that of a normal organism. Any difference in phenotype gives evidence about what the gene normally does.

A collection of strains of a model organism in which, in each strain, a different single gene has been made inoperative. Libraries covering most or all genes are available for some species used as models in research, such as the mouse, the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae and the plant Arabidopsis thaliana, so that a researcher can obtain a ready-made knockout of the gene of interest.

A technique for making a deliberate change at a chosen position in a genome. A guide RNA whose sequence is complementary to the target DNA leads the enzyme Cas9 to that position, where Cas9 cuts both strands of the DNA. The cell's own DNA repair processes then reseal the break, either disrupting the gene or, if a template DNA sequence is supplied, incorporating the intended new sequence. A successful use is the treatment of sickle cell disease by editing a patient's own blood-forming stem cells so that they produce fetal haemoglobin.

A short RNA molecule used in CRISPR–Cas9 editing that binds to Cas9 and contains a sequence of about 20 bases complementary to the target DNA. Base pairing between the guide RNA and the DNA determines where Cas9 cuts; the guide RNA does not itself cut DNA.

Scientists in different countries work under different regulatory systems, so a use of CRISPR that is prohibited in one country may be permitted in another. Because some potential uses (for example editing human embryos so that changes are inherited) raise ethical issues that must be addressed before implementation, there is an international effort to harmonize the regulation of genome editing technologies.

A base sequence in a gene that is identical or similar across a species or across a group of species. Conservation is detected by aligning the sequences of the gene from different individuals or species and finding few differences.

A base sequence that has remained identical or similar over long periods of evolution, so that it is found with little change in groups of organisms that diverged hundreds of millions of years ago. Genes for histones and for ribosomal RNA are examples.

One hypothesis to account for conserved sequences: mutations occur in the sequence at the usual rate, but almost any change impairs the gene product so much that individuals carrying the mutation are removed by natural selection. The sequence appears unchanged because only the original version survives, not because it mutates less often.

The alternative hypothesis to account for conserved sequences: fewer mutations arise in the conserved region in the first place, for example because the sequence is replicated or repaired with unusually high accuracy. The two hypotheses can be distinguished by measuring the rate at which new mutations actually appear in the sequence.

mcqs.q: Part of the base sequence of a gene is GAT TCA GGC ATT before a mutation and GAT TCG GCA TT after it. Which type of gene mutation has occurred?
options: A deletion of one base, which has moved every later base one position along
A substitution of the base A by G at the sixth position in the sequence
A chromosome mutation, because the total amount of DNA has changed
A substitution that has shifted the reading frame of later codons
mcqs.specStatementText: Three kinds of gene mutation: substitution, insertion, deletion
mcqs.explain: Aligning the two sequences shows that the A in the second codon is missing and every base after it has moved up one place; the mutant is one base shorter. This is a deletion.
rationales: Aligning the two sequences shows that the A in the second codon is missing and every base after it has moved up one place; the mutant is one base shorter. This is a deletion.

A student who compares the sequences position by position sees A become G and calls it a substitution. A substitution leaves the length unchanged, but the mutant sequence has 11 bases instead of 12: one base has been deleted and the rest have shifted.

A student who sorts mutations by whether DNA is gained or lost picks this. A change of one base within a gene is a gene mutation (a deletion); chromosome mutations alter the number or structure of whole chromosomes.

A student who attaches frameshift to every mutation picks this. The frame has shifted, but only because a base was removed; a substitution cannot shift the frame because it does not change the number of bases.

mcqs.q: In mRNA the codons GCU, GCC, GCA and GCG all code for alanine. A base substitution in a gene changes the codon GCU in its mRNA to GCC. What is the effect on the polypeptide?
options: Alanine is replaced by a different amino acid at that one position
None: the same amino acid, alanine, is placed at that position
The reading frame shifts, changing all amino acids after it
Every amino acid in the polypeptide is changed to another one
mcqs.specStatementText: A substitution may change one amino acid, or none
mcqs.explain: GCC codes for alanine just as GCU does, so the substitution is silent. This is a consequence of the degeneracy of the genetic code: a base substitution may or may not change a single amino acid.
rationales: A student who treats codons and amino acids as one-to-one picks this. Alanine has four codons, and GCU to GCC is a change between two of them, so the amino acid is unchanged.
GCC codes for alanine just as GCU does, so the substitution is silent. This is a consequence of the degeneracy of the genetic code: a base substitution may or may not change a single amino acid.
A student who thinks any mutation shifts the frame picks this. A substitution replaces one base with another and leaves the number of bases the same, so the frame is not shifted.

A student who both attaches a frameshift to every mutation (as in m04) and pictures a frameshift as scrambling the whole polypeptide picks this. Even a frameshift leaves earlier codons untouched, and a substitution affects at most the single codon it lies in.

mcqs.q: The same gene was sequenced in 1000 people. At one position 62% carry C and 38% carry T, and the two resulting codons code for the same amino acid. How should this difference be described?
options: A rare mutation causing disease in the 38% group
A frameshift mutation that affects later codons
An SNP that leaves the polypeptide unchanged
A substitution that changes one amino acid
mcqs.specStatementText: A substitution may change one amino acid, or none
mcqs.explain: A single base differs between individuals at one position: this is a single-nucleotide polymorphism, the result of a base substitution that has spread in the population. Because both codons specify the same amino acid, the polypeptide is unchanged.
rationales: A student who equates SNP with genetic disease picks this. A variant carried by 38% of people is common, not rare, and both versions code for the same amino acid, so there is no basis for calling it disease-causing.
A student who thinks a substitution shifts the reading frame picks this. One base has been replaced by another, not added or removed, so every codon stays in place.

A single base differs between individuals at one position: this is a single-nucleotide polymorphism, the result of a base substitution that has spread in the population. Because both codons specify the same amino acid, the polypeptide is unchanged.

A student who assumes every codon change alters the amino acid picks this. The stem states that both codons code for the same amino acid, which is possible because of the degeneracy of the genetic code.

mcqs.q: One base is deleted from the fourth codon of a gene coding for a polypeptide of 300 amino acids. What is the most likely consequence?
options: Only the fourth amino acid is altered, so the polypeptide still works normally
Every one of the 300 amino acids is changed, including the first three
The change is a chromosome mutation, so the gene is not transcribed at all
Almost all of the polypeptide is altered and it ceases to function
mcqs.specStatementText: Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
mcqs.explain: Deleting one base shifts the reading frame from the fourth codon onwards, so the remaining 297 codons are regrouped and read as different amino acids until a premature stop codon is reached. A polypeptide altered this extensively is very likely to cease functioning.
rationales: A student who applies the substitution rule of one base, one amino acid picks this. A deletion moves every later base one place, so all the codons after the fourth are regrouped: this is a frameshift.

A student who thinks a frameshift scrambles the whole polypeptide picks this. The ribosome reads the first three codons correctly before it reaches the mutation; only the sequence from the fourth codon onwards is altered.
A student who classes any loss of DNA as a chromosome mutation picks this. The loss of a single base is a gene mutation; the gene is still transcribed and translated, but in a shifted reading frame.

Deleting one base shifts the reading frame from the fourth codon onwards, so the remaining 297 codons are regrouped and read as different amino acids until a premature stop codon is reached. A polypeptide altered this extensively is very likely to cease functioning.

mcqs.q: Two copies of a gene are mutated at the same point in the coding sequence. In copy X three consecutive bases are inserted; in copy Y one base is inserted. Which comparison is correct?
options: X keeps the reading frame so the codons after it are unchanged, but Y shifts the frame for every later codon
Both X and Y shift the reading frame, so both of the polypeptides are likely to cease to function
Both X and Y alter just one amino acid at the insertion point, leaving the rest unchanged
Y changes every amino acid, including those before the insertion, whereas X adds just one amino acid
mcqs.specStatementText: Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
mcqs.explain: Three bases is a whole codon, so in X the codons after the insertion are grouped exactly as before: the polypeptide gains one amino acid (possibly with one adjacent amino acid altered) and the rest is unchanged. One extra base in Y is not a multiple of three, so every later codon is regrouped: a frameshift that is likely to abolish function.
rationales: Three bases is a whole codon, so in X the codons after the insertion are grouped exactly as before: the polypeptide gains one amino acid (possibly with one adjacent amino acid altered) and the rest is unchanged. One extra base in Y is not a multiple of three, so every later codon is regrouped: a frameshift that is likely to abolish function.

A student who thinks every insertion causes a frameshift picks this. The frame shifts only when the number of bases inserted is not a multiple of three, so X, with three bases inserted, keeps the frame.

A student who assumes one base change means one amino acid change picks this. It is roughly true for X, but the single extra base in Y regroups every codon after it, changing the whole of the rest of the polypeptide.

A student who thinks a frameshift alters the amino acids before the mutation as well picks this. The X clause is correct, but in Y the ribosome reads the codons before the insertion exactly as before; only the codons after it are regrouped.

mcqs.q: Why is a polypeptide likely to cease functioning when several hundred bases are deleted from the middle of its gene?
options: Only because a deletion of any size shifts the reading frame of every later codon
So many amino acids are missing that the polypeptide cannot fold into its working shape
Only the amino acids coded by the deleted bases are missing; the rest still folds as normal
The amino acids coded before the deletion are also changed by the loss of bases
mcqs.specStatementText: Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
mcqs.explain: A major deletion removes a large section of the coding sequence, so a long run of amino acids is absent from the polypeptide. Even if the reading frame happens to be preserved, a polypeptide missing so much of its sequence is unlikely to fold into a functional shape.
rationales: A student who thinks every deletion is a frameshift picks this. If the number of bases deleted is a multiple of three the frame is unchanged, yet the polypeptide still loses many amino acids and is likely to cease to function for that reason.

A major deletion removes a large section of the coding sequence, so a long run of amino acids is absent from the polypeptide. Even if the reading frame happens to be preserved, a polypeptide missing so much of its sequence is unlikely to fold into a functional shape.

A student who assumes the effect of a deletion is confined to the mutation point, as for a single-base change, picks this. Several hundred bases code for a hundred or more amino acids (three bases per amino acid), and losing that much of the sequence prevents the polypeptide from folding into its functional shape, even if the reading frame is preserved.

A student who thinks any change spreads back along the polypeptide picks this. Codons before the deletion are read exactly as before; the damage lies in the large section that is missing and, if the frame is shifted, in the sequence after it.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the causes of gene mutation is correct?
options: Gene mutations arise only in cells that are exposed to a mutagen
Microwaves and radio waves are mutagenic just like X-rays
Replication errors can cause mutation without a mutagen
Proofreading by DNA polymerase corrects every error
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutagens, and copying errors, cause mutation
mcqs.explain: Gene mutation is caused by mutagens and by errors in DNA replication or repair. DNA polymerase occasionally pairs a base wrongly, and a small fraction of these errors escape proofreading and repair and become permanent mutations.
rationales: A student who knows mutagens as the cause of mutation picks this. Mutagens raise the rate, but replication and repair errors produce a background rate of mutation in cells that have met no mutagen at all.

A student who treats all radiation as dangerous to DNA picks this. Only ionizing radiation, such as X-rays and gamma rays, and ultraviolet light have enough energy to alter DNA; microwaves and radio waves do not.

Gene mutation is caused by mutagens and by errors in DNA replication or repair. DNA polymerase occasionally pairs a base wrongly, and a small fraction of these errors escape proofreading and repair and become permanent mutations.
A student who turns a very low error rate into a zero error rate picks this. Proofreading and repair correct most errors, but not all, which is why replication errors are a genuine cause of mutation.

mcqs.q: Cultures of cells were exposed separately to (i) ultraviolet light, (ii) visible light and (iii) nitrous acid, a chemical that alters bases in DNA. Which treatments are expected to raise the mutation rate above the background rate?
options: (i), (ii) and (iii), because light and chemicals both damage DNA
(iii) only, because radiation from non-radioactive sources is harmless
None of them, because DNA repair enzymes correct all of the damage
(i) and (iii), because both chemically alter the bases in DNA
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutagens, and copying errors, cause mutation
mcqs.explain: Ultraviolet light is a mutagenic form of radiation (it causes adjacent thymine bases to bond together) and nitrous acid is a chemical mutagen that alters bases so that they mispair. Visible light does not have enough energy to change DNA.
rationales: A student who assumes all radiation is mutagenic includes visible light. Visible light does not carry enough energy to alter DNA chemically, so it is not a mutagen; only the ultraviolet light and the chemical raise the mutation rate.

A student who thinks only nuclear radiation is mutagenic picks this. Ultraviolet light is a mutagenic form of radiation whatever its source; sunlight is the main cause of the mutations that lead to skin cancer.
A student who believes repair is perfect picks this. Repair enzymes correct most damage, but mutagens increase the damage so much that more errors escape, and the mutation rate rises measurably.

Ultraviolet light is a mutagenic form of radiation (it causes adjacent thymine bases to bond together) and nitrous acid is a chemical mutagen that alters bases so that they mispair. Visible light does not have enough energy to change DNA.

mcqs.q: Which statement about randomness in mutation is correct?
options: Mutations can occur anywhere in the genome, but some bases have a higher probability of mutating than others
Mutations can occur anywhere in the genome, and every base has an identical probability of mutating
Mutations occur in the genes an organism needs to change when its environment changes
Mutations occur only at those bases in the genome that a mutagen has chemically damaged
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutation is random, but not evenly spread
mcqs.explain: Mutation is random in the sense that no natural mechanism directs a change to a particular base for the purpose of changing a trait; it is not uniform, because the chemistry of some bases and sequences (for example methylated cytosine) makes them mutation hotspots.
rationales: Mutation is random in the sense that no natural mechanism directs a change to a particular base for the purpose of changing a trait; it is not uniform, because the chemistry of some bases and sequences (for example methylated cytosine) makes them mutation hotspots.
A student who reads random as equally likely picks this. Randomness refers to the lack of direction towards a useful outcome; some bases mutate much more often than others.
A student who thinks organisms mutate in response to need picks this. No natural mechanism is known for making a deliberate change to a particular base with the purpose of changing a trait.
A student who ties every mutation to a mutagen picks this. Errors in replication or repair cause mutations at bases that no mutagen has touched, anywhere in the genome.

mcqs.q: A bacterial culture that has never been exposed to the antibiotic streptomycin is found to contain about one resistant cell per 10⁷ cells. When streptomycin is added, the resistant cells survive and the culture soon consists almost entirely of resistant cells. What do these observations show?
options: The antibiotic caused the bacteria to mutate the gene that gives resistance because they needed it in order to survive
The resistance mutation arose by chance before exposure, and the antibiotic then selected the cells carrying it
Most mutations in bacteria are beneficial, which is why the resistance spread through the culture so quickly
The resistance allele was created by recombination during reproduction rather than by mutation
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutation is random, but not evenly spread
mcqs.explain: Resistant cells were already present at a low frequency in a culture that had never met the antibiotic, so the mutation must have occurred at random beforehand. Adding streptomycin did not create resistance; it killed the sensitive cells and left the resistant ones to multiply.
rationales: A student who believes mutation is directed by need picks this. The resistant cells existed before the antibiotic was added, so the antibiotic cannot have caused the mutation; it only selected the cells that already carried it.

Resistant cells were already present at a low frequency in a culture that had never met the antibiotic, so the mutation must have occurred at random beforehand. Adding streptomycin did not create resistance; it killed the sensitive cells and left the resistant ones to multiply.

A student who thinks mutation is mostly helpful picks this. Resistance was present in only one cell in ten million, consistent with a rare beneficial mutation among many harmful or neutral ones; it spread because selection removed the sensitive cells.

A student who credits reproduction with making new alleles picks this. Bacteria in the culture reproduce asexually, and in any organism recombination only reshuffles existing alleles: a new allele can arise only by mutation.

mcqs.q: Which statement about mutations in germ cells and somatic cells is correct?
options: A mutation in a skin cell can be inherited by the person's children
Every mutation in a somatic cell causes that cell to become cancerous
A mutation in a germ cell can be passed on to the offspring
A mutation in one liver cell spreads to every body cell
mcqs.specStatementText: Germ cell mutations are inherited; somatic mutations stay in the body
mcqs.explain: Germ cells give rise to gametes, so a mutated gene in a germ cell can be passed to the next generation, where it will be present in every cell of the offspring. This is how mutation adds inherited variation to a species.
rationales: A student who treats all of a person's DNA as heritable picks this. Skin cells are somatic cells: their DNA is never passed to a gamete, so the mutation dies with the individual.
A student who equates somatic mutation with cancer picks this. Cancer follows mutations in the genes that control the cell cycle; most somatic mutations are silent or harmless.

Germ cells give rise to gametes, so a mutated gene in a germ cell can be passed to the next generation, where it will be present in every cell of the offspring. This is how mutation adds inherited variation to a species.
A student who generalises from inherited mutations picks this. A somatic mutation is copied only into the descendants of the cell in which it occurred, not into other cells of the body.

mcqs.q: A mutation occurs in a gene that controls the cell cycle in one cell lining a man's colon. Which statement about the consequences is correct?
options: The mutation will be passed on to all of the man's children
The mutation will spread to every cell in the man's body
The cell has become cancerous, as does every mutated somatic cell
The cell may divide uncontrollably and form a tumour
mcqs.specStatementText: Germ cell mutations are inherited; somatic mutations stay in the body
mcqs.explain: Genes controlling the cell cycle keep cell division under control. A mutation in such a gene in a somatic cell can allow the cell and its descendants to divide without restraint, which is how cancer begins; several such mutations are usually needed before a tumour forms.
rationales: A student who thinks any mutation is heritable picks this. A colon cell is a somatic cell, so its mutation cannot enter a sperm cell and is not inherited.
A student who expects a mutation to spread through the body picks this. The mutation is copied only into the descendants of the one mutated cell when it divides.
A student who equates somatic mutation with cancer picks this. Most somatic mutations do not cause cancer, and even a mutation in a cell-cycle gene raises the risk rather than guaranteeing a tumour.

Genes controlling the cell cycle keep cell division under control. A mutation in such a gene in a somatic cell can allow the cell and its descendants to divide without restraint, which is how cancer begins; several such mutations are usually needed before a tumour forms.

mcqs.q: Why is gene mutation described as the original source of all genetic variation?
options: New alleles arise only by mutation; meiosis and fertilization just recombine alleles that already exist
Crossing over in meiosis creates new alleles, and mutation adds to the variation they produce
Most mutations are beneficial, so each one adds a useful new variant to the species
Organisms generate new alleles whenever their environment demands a new trait from them
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutation is where all new alleles come from
mcqs.explain: Every allele of every gene began as a mutation in a germ cell of some ancestor. Meiosis and fertilization produce new combinations of alleles, which adds variation among individuals, but they cannot produce a new allele.
rationales: Every allele of every gene began as a mutation in a germ cell of some ancestor. Meiosis and fertilization produce new combinations of alleles, which adds variation among individuals, but they cannot produce a new allele.
A student who thinks crossing over makes new genes picks this. Crossing over exchanges existing alleles between chromatids; it produces new combinations, not new alleles.

A student who thinks mutation is mostly helpful picks this. Most mutations are harmful or neutral for the individual; mutation is the source of variation regardless of whether a particular mutation is useful.
A student who believes mutation is directed picks this. Mutations occur at random with respect to their usefulness; the environment selects among variants that already exist.

mcqs.q: A direct-to-consumer genetic test reports that a healthy woman carries an SNP associated with a risk of type 2 diabetes 1.5 times higher than that of people without it. Which interpretation is correct?
options: She will certainly develop type 2 diabetes in later life, because she carries the genetic variant that causes the disease
She is more likely than non-carriers to develop the disease, but may never do so; expert interpretation is needed
The test has diagnosed type 2 diabetes in her, so she should begin treatment for the disease immediately
The SNP is a rare disease-causing error in her DNA, so she has inherited a genetic disease from one parent
mcqs.specStatementText: Mutation is where all new alleles come from
mcqs.explain: The result describes an altered probability, not an outcome. Whether she develops type 2 diabetes also depends on other genes, diet, activity and chance. This is the NOS point: without expert interpretation, information from commercial genetic tests can be problematic.
rationales: A student who reads a risk as a prediction picks this. A 1.5-fold risk means the disease is somewhat more likely, not certain, and many carriers never develop it.

The result describes an altered probability, not an outcome. Whether she develops type 2 diabetes also depends on other genes, diet, activity and chance. This is the NOS point: without expert interpretation, information from commercial genetic tests can be problematic.
A student who treats a genetic test like a blood test picks this. The test read her DNA variants; it did not measure her blood glucose or detect any present disease, and she is healthy.
A student who equates SNP with a defective gene picks this. SNPs are common variants; this one shifts the probability of a complex disease and is not a disease-causing mutation.

mcqs.q: Researchers want to investigate the function of gene Z in mice. They obtain a strain from a knockout library in which gene Z is inoperative. How should they use it?
options: Conclude that Z has no function if the knockout mice appear normal
Check first that the whole of gene Z has been cut out of the chromosome
Compare the phenotype of the knockout mice with that of normal mice
Block the protein made by gene Z in adult mice and observe the effect
mcqs.specStatementText: Knock a gene out to see what it does
mcqs.explain: Gene knockout investigates function by making the gene inoperative and observing what changes. Any difference between the knockout and normal mice, in structure, physiology or behaviour, is evidence about what the product of gene Z normally does.
rationales: A student who reads a null result at face value picks this. An unchanged phenotype may mean another gene compensates or that the function is needed only under conditions not tested, so it does not show that Z is functionless.
A student who thinks knockout means physical removal picks this. A gene is knocked out when it is changed so that it is inoperative; its DNA may still be present.

Gene knockout investigates function by making the gene inoperative and observing what changes. Any difference between the knockout and normal mice, in structure, physiology or behaviour, is evidence about what the product of gene Z normally does.

A student who confuses inhibiting a protein with knocking out a gene picks this. The knockout strain makes no functional product of Z in any cell, so there is no protein to block; the comparison is between organisms.

mcqs.q: Mice in which gene P has been knocked out show no detectable difference from normal mice under standard laboratory conditions. What is the best conclusion?
options: P has no function, because removing its product produced no change in the mice's phenotype
The knockout did not work, because the sequence of P is still present in the genome
The protein made by P is still active because only the gene, not the protein, was altered
P may have a function masked by another gene or shown only in untested conditions
mcqs.specStatementText: Knock a gene out to see what it does
mcqs.explain: Absence of a visible change does not show absence of function. Another gene with a similar product may compensate for the loss, the function may matter only under stress, infection or at other life stages, or the effect may be too subtle for the tests used.
rationales: A student who takes a null result as proof picks this. The knockout can only reveal functions that produce a difference under the conditions examined; redundancy and untested conditions can hide a real function.
A student who thinks a knocked-out gene must be absent from the DNA picks this. A gene is knocked out when it is made inoperative; its sequence can remain in the chromosome.
A student who thinks knockout acts on the protein picks this. Making the gene inoperative means no functional protein is produced, so there is no active protein from P in the knockout mice.

Absence of a visible change does not show absence of function. Another gene with a similar product may compensate for the loss, the function may matter only under stress, infection or at other life stages, or the effect may be too subtle for the tests used.

mcqs.q: In CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing, what determines the position in the genome at which the DNA is cut?
options: The base sequence of the guide RNA, which pairs with the complementary sequence in the target DNA
The active site of the Cas9 enzyme, which recognises the target DNA base sequence directly
The guide RNA, which cuts both strands of the DNA at the position where it binds to it
The sequence of the new bases that Cas9 itself inserts into the gene to rewrite it
mcqs.specStatementText: CRISPR–Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA leads it
mcqs.explain: The guide RNA contains about 20 bases complementary to the target. Base pairing between the guide RNA and the DNA holds Cas9 at that one position, where Cas9 cuts both strands. Changing the guide RNA sequence changes the site that is cut.
rationales: The guide RNA contains about 20 bases complementary to the target. Base pairing between the guide RNA and the DNA holds Cas9 at that one position, where Cas9 cuts both strands. Changing the guide RNA sequence changes the site that is cut.
A student who expects specificity to come from the enzyme picks this. Cas9 cuts wherever it is taken; the target is chosen by the guide RNA, not by the enzyme's active site.
A student who gives the guide RNA the active role picks this. The guide RNA does locate the target, but it cannot cut DNA; the enzyme Cas9 makes the cut.
A student who thinks Cas9 writes the new sequence picks this. Cas9 only cuts; any new sequence is copied in by the cell's repair processes, and the cut site is set by the guide RNA.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of the successful use of CRISPR–Cas9 gene editing?
options: Editing the skin cells of adults with sickle cell disease so that all their own children inherit the corrected gene
Editing the blood-forming stem cells of patients with sickle cell disease so that they produce fetal haemoglobin
Using Cas9 itself both to cut out the faulty bases and to write the corrected sequence into the gene
Using guide RNA on its own to cut out the faulty base from the gene in a patient's blood cells
mcqs.specStatementText: CRISPR–Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA leads it
mcqs.explain: In this treatment, approved in 2023, a patient's own blood-forming stem cells are edited with CRISPR–Cas9 so that they switch on production of fetal haemoglobin, which prevents red blood cells from sickling. The edited cells are returned to the patient.
rationales: A student who thinks somatic edits are inherited picks this. Edits to skin cells are never passed to gametes, so this could not work; the real treatment edits the patient's own blood-forming cells for the patient's own benefit.

In this treatment, approved in 2023, a patient's own blood-forming stem cells are edited with CRISPR–Cas9 so that they switch on production of fetal haemoglobin, which prevents red blood cells from sickling. The edited cells are returned to the patient.

A student who thinks Cas9 both cuts and rewrites the gene picks this. Cas9 only makes a double-strand break; the change to the sequence is produced by the cell's own repair processes, with or without a supplied template, so this is not how any CRISPR treatment works.
A student who gives the guide RNA the cutting role picks this. The guide RNA only locates the target by base pairing; without Cas9 no cut is made and no edit occurs.

mcqs.q: In 2018 a scientist announced the birth of babies whose genomes had been edited with CRISPR–Cas9 at the embryo stage. The work was condemned by scientists worldwide and the scientist was later imprisoned under his own country's laws. Why is there an international effort to harmonize the regulation of genome editing?
options: A single worldwide law on genome editing exists and only needs to be enforced
Once embryo editing is shown to be safe there will be no ethical issue left to regulate
Regulation is national, so a use banned in one country may be legal in another
Editing an embryo is the same as editing adult somatic cells, so no new rules are needed
mcqs.specStatementText: CRISPR–Cas9 cuts DNA where a guide RNA leads it
mcqs.explain: Regulation is national, so what is prohibited in one country may be legal or unregulated in another and research could move to the least restrictive jurisdiction. Harmonizing regulation aims to ensure that the ethical issues raised by uses such as heritable embryo editing are addressed before implementation anywhere.
rationales: A student who assumes a global authority already governs this picks this. No such law exists; the scientist was punished under national law, and it is precisely because rules differ between countries that harmonization is being sought.

A student who equates ethical with safe picks this. Consent of future generations, fairness of access and the acceptability of altering human embryos are ethical issues that remain even if the procedure is safe.

Regulation is national, so what is prohibited in one country may be legal or unregulated in another and research could move to the least restrictive jurisdiction. Harmonizing regulation aims to ensure that the ethical issues raised by uses such as heritable embryo editing are addressed before implementation anywhere.

A student who thinks somatic edits are inherited sees no difference between the two. Edits to an embryo enter every cell including the germ line and are passed to descendants; edits to an adult's somatic cells are not, which is why embryo editing raises distinct ethical issues.

mcqs.q: The gene for histone H4 codes for an almost identical amino acid sequence in peas and in cattle, whose lineages diverged over a billion years ago. Which pair of hypotheses could account for this?
options: The DNA of the gene is protected so that no mutation can occur in it in either organism
The gene is not used in either organism, so nothing has changed it since they diverged
Each organism deliberately restores any base that changes, because it needs the histone protein
Selection removes mutations that impair the protein, or the gene mutates more slowly
mcqs.specStatementText: Two hypotheses for why some sequences barely change
mcqs.explain: These are the two hypotheses for conserved sequences. Under the functional-requirement hypothesis mutations arise but almost any change to histone H4 is so damaging that carriers are eliminated by natural selection; under the slower-mutation-rate hypothesis fewer mutations arise in the sequence in the first place.
rationales: A student who hears conserved as protected picks this. Mutations can occur anywhere in a genome; a highly conserved sequence is one in which changes either arise more slowly or are removed by selection, not one that cannot mutate.

A student who reasons that unused things stay intact picks this. Sequences that are not used are free to accumulate mutations and diverge quickly; histone H4 is essential in every eukaryotic cell, which is why change is not tolerated.

A student who believes organisms direct changes to their DNA picks this. No natural mechanism is known for making a deliberate change to a particular base for the purpose of changing or preserving a trait.

These are the two hypotheses for conserved sequences. Under the functional-requirement hypothesis mutations arise but almost any change to histone H4 is so damaging that carriers are eliminated by natural selection; under the slower-mutation-rate hypothesis fewer mutations arise in the sequence in the first place.

mcqs.q: The rate at which new mutations appear per generation was measured directly in a highly conserved gene and in a gene that is not conserved. The rates were the same, but far fewer of the new mutations in the conserved gene persisted in later generations. Which hypothesis do the data support?
options: Functional requirement: mutations arise at the normal rate but carriers are removed by natural selection
Slower mutation rate: the conserved gene is protected from mutation, so fewer changes arise in it
Lack of use: the conserved gene is inactive, so mutations in it have no effect and persist
Beneficial mutation: most new mutations in the conserved gene improve it and so spread rapidly
mcqs.specStatementText: Two hypotheses for why some sequences barely change
mcqs.explain: Equal rates of new mutation rule out the slower-mutation-rate hypothesis for this gene. Mutations arise as often as elsewhere but do not persist, which is what the functional-requirement hypothesis predicts: almost any change to the gene product is harmful, so carriers are eliminated and the original sequence is preserved.
rationales: Equal rates of new mutation rule out the slower-mutation-rate hypothesis for this gene. Mutations arise as often as elsewhere but do not persist, which is what the functional-requirement hypothesis predicts: almost any change to the gene product is harmful, so carriers are eliminated and the original sequence is preserved.
A student who assumes conservation means mutations cannot occur picks this. The measured rate of new mutations was the same in both genes, so the data contradict a slower mutation rate here.

A student who thinks conserved sequences are unused picks this. The data show the opposite: mutations in the conserved gene did not persist, which indicates strong selection against change, not indifference to it.

A student who thinks most mutations are beneficial picks this. If the mutations were beneficial they would persist and spread; instead they disappeared, showing that they were harmful and selected against.

Insertions and deletions usually wreck the polypeptide
Mutagens, and copying errors, cause mutation
Mutation is random, but not evenly spread
Germ cell mutations are inherited; somatic mutations stay in the body
Mutation is where all new alleles come from
Knock a gene out to see what it does

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Insertions and deletions are tested only through generic sequences invented for the items and through the general consequences (frameshift, major insertion or deletion). No named disease, gene or organism is used as an example of an insertion or deletion mutation.

Gene knockout is treated only as making a gene inoperative so that the phenotype of the knockout organism can be compared with the normal organism, plus the existence of knockout libraries for model species. No item asks how a knockout is made: homologous recombination, embryonic stem cells, selectable markers and the CRISPR-based knockout workflow are all left out.

CRISPR–Cas9 is described only as a gene-editing tool: a guide RNA directs the Cas9 enzyme to cut DNA at a complementary target sequence and the cell's own repair processes then produce the edit. The natural function of CRISPR sequences and Cas proteins as an adaptive defence in bacteria and archaea, spacers, PAM sequences and the prokaryotic immunity mechanism are not mentioned in any object.
